clinicalPearls: A life-threatening acute hypersensitivity reaction during anaesthesia, often presenting abruptly with cardiovascular collapse rather than the skin signs seen in awake patients
Common triggers include neuromuscular blocking agents, antibiotics, latex, and chlorhexidine, with contrast and colloids as additional causes
Cardiovascular features (profound hypotension, tachycardia, and collapse) and respiratory features (bronchospasm, high airway pressures, desaturation) predominate under drapes
Cutaneous signs such as flushing, urticaria, and angioedema may be absent, masked, or noticed late because the patient is covered
Adrenaline (epinephrine) is the first-line treatment, titrated to severity, alongside stopping the likely trigger, giving oxygen, and aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation
Refractory cases may need escalating vasopressor support, and cardiac arrest is managed with standard advanced life support with prolonged effort as needed
A mast cell tryptase level taken during and after the reaction supports the diagnosis, and the patient must be referred for allergy testing to identify the culprit
Clear documentation and patient warning about the responsible agent are essential to prevent recurrence at future anaesthetics
reference.pathophysiology: Perioperative anaphylaxis is usually an immediate hypersensitivity reaction, often IgE-mediated, in which prior sensitisation leads to cross-linking of IgE on mast cells and basophils upon re-exposure to an antigen. Some reactions are non-IgE-mediated or result from direct mast cell activation. Degranulation releases histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, and other mediators that cause vasodilation, increased vascular permeability with fluid shift, bronchoconstriction, and myocardial depression. The result is rapid loss of intravascular volume, distributive shock, and airway compromise. Adrenaline counteracts these effects through vasoconstriction, bronchodilation, and stabilisation of mast cells.
additionalInvestigations: Serial mast cell tryptase levels during the reaction and after recovery
Continuous ECG, blood pressure, and oxygenation monitoring
Arterial blood gas to assess oxygenation and acidosis
Referral for later skin and specific IgE allergy testing to identify the trigger
Review of all agents and materials administered around the time of the reaction
redFlags: Sudden cardiovascular collapse or cardiac arrest during anaesthesia
Severe bronchospasm with high airway pressures and difficulty ventilating
Profound refractory hypotension despite fluids and vasopressors
Rapidly progressive airway swelling or angioedema threatening the airway
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition and early adrenaline most patients recover, but delayed treatment or severe refractory shock can be fatal or cause hypoxic organ injury; identifying and avoiding the trigger prevents recurrence.
pitfalls: Delaying adrenaline while awaiting confirmation of the diagnosis
Expecting skin signs and dismissing anaphylaxis when they are absent under drapes
Failing to send timed tryptase samples or to refer for allergy testing
Under-resuscitating the large fluid deficit caused by capillary leak
Not documenting or warning the patient about the causative agent
management: Give adrenaline immediately as first-line treatment, titrated intramuscularly or intravenously to the severity of the reaction, and call for help
Stop administration of the likely trigger, such as a neuromuscular blocking agent, antibiotic, chlorhexidine or latex
Secure the airway, deliver high-flow oxygen and relieve bronchospasm with inhaled or nebulised bronchodilators
Provide aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation to counter distributive shock, vasodilation and capillary fluid shift
Escalate refractory shock with vasopressor infusions such as noradrenaline or vasopressin, and consider glucagon in patients taking beta-blockers
Manage cardiac arrest with standard advanced life support, using prolonged resuscitation efforts as needed
Give adjunctive corticosteroids and antihistamines after initial resuscitation and observe for a biphasic reaction
Take serial mast cell tryptase samples and refer for later skin and specific IgE allergy testing to identify and document the trigger for future avoidance
